{{Short description|Smallest number of edges of an equivalent polygonal path for a knot}}
[[File:Trefoil valknut cropped.png|thumb|240px|[[Trefoil knot|2,3 torus (or trefoil) knot]] has a stick number of six.]]
In the [[knot theory|mathematical theory of knots]], the '''stick number''' is a [[knot invariant]] that intuitively gives the smallest number of straight "sticks" stuck end to end needed to form a knot. Specifically, given any knot <math>K</math>, the stick number of <math>K</math>, denoted by <math>\operatorname{stick}(K)</math>, is the smallest number of edges of a [[polygonal path]] equivalent {{nowrap|to <math>K</math>.}} A related quantity is the '''equilateral stick number''', the smallest number of edges of the same length that are required to form a knot. It is not currently known whether the equilateral stick number is the same as the stick number for every knot.

==Known values==
Six is the lowest stick number for any nontrivial knot. There are few knots whose stick number can be determined exactly. Gyo Taek Jin determined the stick number of a <math>(p,q)</math>-[[torus knot]] <math>T(p,q)</math> in case the parameters <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are not too far from each other:<ref>{{harvnb|Jin|1997}}</ref>
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\operatorname{stick}(T(p,q)) = 2q</math>, if <math>2 \le p < q \le 2p.</math>}}

The same result was found independently around the same time by a research group around [[Colin Adams (mathematician)|Colin Adams]], but for a smaller range of parameters.<ref>{{harvnb|Adams|Brennan|Greilsheimer|Woo|1997}}</ref>

There are certain knots for which the upper bound and lower bound of the stick number are the same, such that the stick number is known exactly. These include 3<sub>1</sub> with a stick number of 6, 4<sub>1</sub> (7), all 5 and 6 crossing knots (8), and all 7 crossing knots (9). The 8 crossing knots 16 through 21 in [[Alexander-Briggs notation]] (8 or 9), and 9-crossing knots 29, 34, 35, and 39 through 49 (9), and 10<sub>124</sub> (10, a torus knot) have known crossing numbers. There are 19 additional non-alternating 11- and 13-crossing knots with a stick number of exactly 10.<ref name="b844">{{cite arXiv | last1=Cantarella | first1=Jason | last2=Rechnitzer | first2=Andrew | last3=Schumacher | first3=Henrik | last4=Shonkwiler | first4=Clayton | title=New Upper Bounds for Stick Numbers | date=2025-08-25 | class=math.GT | eprint=2508.18263 }}</ref>
[[File:StickKnot9 35.png|thumb|alt=A 9_35 knot made of 9 sticks|Rendering of a 9<sub>35</sub> knot with a stick number of 9, from coordinates found by Shonkwiler and Eddy.<ref name="q487">{{cite journal | last1=Eddy | first1=Thomas D. | last2=Shonkwiler | first2=Clayton | title=New stick number bounds from random sampling of confined polygons | journal=Experimental Mathematics | volume=31 | issue=4 | date=2022-10-02 | issn=1058-6458 | doi=10.1080/10586458.2021.1926000 | doi-access=free | pages=1373–1395 | arxiv=1909.00917 }}</ref>]]

==Bounds==
[[File:Square knot sum of trefoils stick number.png|thumb|Square knot {{=}} trefoil + trefoil reflection.<!--6 + 6 - 3 = 9 ≥ 8.-->]]
The stick number of a [[knot sum]] can be upper bounded by the stick numbers of the summands:<ref>{{harvnb|Adams|Brennan|Greilsheimer|Woo|1997}}, {{harvnb|Jin|1997}}</ref>
<math display=block>\text{stick}(K_1\#K_2)\le \text{stick}(K_1)+ \text{stick}(K_2)-3 \, </math>

==Related invariants==
The stick number of a knot <math>K</math> is related to its [[crossing number (knot theory)|crossing number]] <math>c(K)</math> by the following inequalities:<ref>{{harvnb|Negami|1991}}, {{harvnb|Calvo|2001}}, {{harvnb|Huh|Oh|2011}}</ref>
<math display=block>\frac12(7+\sqrt{8\,\text{c}(K)+1}) \le \text{stick}(K)\le \frac32 (c(K)+1).</math>

These inequalities are both tight for the [[trefoil knot]], which has a crossing number of 3 and a stick number of 6. The upper bound on the stick number does not apply to the [[unknot]], which has crossing number 0 but stick number 3.

==Optical Illusions==
[[File:Right-handed interlaced pentagram.svg|thumb|A right-handed interlaced pentagram, which is a diagram of a trefoil knot but cannot be realized in three dimensions without curving the line segments.]]
Knots can be drawn with fewer straight line segments than their stick number suggests should be possible. These diagrams are optical illusions, and three-dimensional embeddings of such knots would require the apparent lines to curve. An example is a five-segment interlaced [[pentagram]], which is a valid diagram of the trefoil knot but cannot be realized with straight line segments. At least six straight line segments are required to embed a trefoil knot.
